newsitem.title: ZAIRE: TALKS COULD SPARE ZAIRE ARMY THEIR BIGGEST DEFEAT.
newsitem.headline: TALKS COULD SPARE ZAIRE ARMY THEIR BIGGEST DEFEAT.

text.p: President Mobutu Sese Seko's ragged Zairean army could be spared final defeat in the capital if negotiations halt rebel advances on the city, military analysts said.
Information Minister Kin-Kiey Mulumba said on Wednesday Mobutu would soon meet Laurent Kabila whose rebels have seized half the country and are moving on the capital.
Kabila has been in South Africa, which has been attempting to mediate talks to halt the fighting, and met President Nelson Mandela in Cape Town on Wednesday.
Military analysts said an armed confrontation in Kinshasa looked likely to be a rout for Mobutu's forces, like previous rounds in the six-month-old rebellion.
"There is no reason to expect they will do better in Kinshasa," one analyst said.
Zaire's emergency rule prime minister, General Likulia Bolongo, has vowed that the army will fight to defend the capital and all territory remaining in government control.
President Mobutu's elite presidential guard, as well as much of the army's remaining weaponry are concentrated in Kinshasa and its eastern outskirts.
But firepower and reinforcements have failed consistently to motivate troops into resisting the rebels in the past.
Military analysts now place guerrillas about 600 km (400 miles) east of the capital around the diamond trading town of Tshikapa not far from the Angolan border.

The capture of towns as far away as 400 km in Bandundu Province which borders Kinshasa's eastern flank, could be enough, some analysts believe, to unleash panic in the capital and precipitate the final demise of the Zairean army.

"Up to 50 per cent of the capital's population originates from the province of Bandundu. If the rebels take Kikwit (350 km from the capital) it would have serious psychological repercussions on Kinshasa," one military analyst told Reuters.
The neighbouring provinces of Lower Zaire on the east as well as Bandundu provide Kinshasa with most of its food, electricity, petrol and other supplies.
Should the rebels surround the city, as many fear, the risk of social tensions exploding is real.
"There is a likelihood of food shortages in Kinshasa soon," said the Western analyst, who asked not to be named.
Mobutu's unarmed opponents in the capital are waging a parallel campaign of civil disorder and have promised to continue anti-Mobutu actions next week.
While both the civil opposition and rebels have Mobutu as their common enemy, they have failed so far to see eye to eye.
Political analysts say the civil campaign seems increasingly aimed at impressing on the rebels that the civil opposition cannot be ignored.
Kabila told reporters on Wednesday his forces would reach Kinshasa within three weeks. "In three weeks, and I'm very serious," he said in answer to a shouted question.
Most analysts believe it could take rebels some time to consolidate positions they hold, and move in adequate numbers to surround the capital.
Military and other sources fear that before the rebels arrived the remnants of the government army, who have looted their way home from defeats in the east, would have made their way to Kinshasa.
"There are thousands of them and most of them are still armed. That is another destabilising factor," an analyst said.
